prompt: How many route tables does one subnet use at a time?
hint: Lesson 16 found the nine subnets using one without being told.

choices.text: As many as are associated with it, read in turn
choices.why: A subnet is associated with one table at a time; associating another replaces the first.

choices.text: One: the main table, unless another is associated
choices.why: Right. A subnet with no association of its own uses the main table implicitly.

choices.text: None, until one is associated
choices.why: That would leave a new subnet unable to route even inside the VPC. The main table covers it from the start.

choices.text: One for each zone the VPC spans
choices.why: Zones do not have route tables; subnets do. The shop has one private table per zone because it chose to.

prompt: A machine in `app-b` sends a packet to `10.20.100.5`, a database in `data-a`, in another zone. Which route of `app-b`'s table carries it?
hint: Which range is `10.20.100.5` inside?

choices.text: The NAT gateway of zone b, since `data-a` is in another zone
choices.why: A NAT gateway is the way out of the VPC. Another zone of the same VPC is still inside it.

choices.text: None: crossing zones needs a peering connection
choices.why: Peering joins two VPCs (lesson 20). The zones of one VPC are joined by the `local` route.

choices.text: `local`, which every table of the VPC carries
choices.why: Right. `10.20.100.5` is inside `10.20.0.0/16`, and `local` covers every subnet of the VPC whatever its zone.

choices.text: The internet gateway, out and back in
choices.why: The packet never leaves the VPC: the `/16` is more specific than `0.0.0.0/0`, and `app-b` has no route to the internet gateway anyway.

prompt: After `17-routes.sh`, somebody fixes a problem quickly by adding `0.0.0.0/0` to the internet gateway in the MAIN route table. Today nothing changes. What has changed for next month?
hint: Which subnets use the main table, today and later?

choices.text: The three public subnets get a second way out
choices.why: They use the `public` table, associated by name; the main table does not apply to them.

choices.text: A subnet created without an association is public from its first minute
choices.why: Right. Every subnet has an explicit table today, so nothing moves now; a new one lands in the main table, which now opens onto the internet.

choices.text: The private subnets start sending their traffic straight to the internet gateway
choices.why: Each private subnet is associated with its zone's table, which still points at its NAT gateway.

choices.text: Nothing, since AWS refuses a route to an internet gateway in the main table
choices.why: AWS accepts it; the default VPC's main table carries exactly that route. That is why the habit of leaving it private matters.

prompt: The destination that contains every IPv4 address, and so the route a packet takes when nothing more specific matches, is written ___.
hint: A prefix of length zero.

prompt: Which of these is true of an internet gateway?
hint: Compare it with a NAT gateway on two points: zone and price.

choices.text: It lives in one zone, so it fails with that zone
choices.why: That is the NAT gateway. AWS runs the internet gateway across every zone of the region.

choices.text: It is charged by the hour, like a NAT gateway
choices.why: An internet gateway has no hourly charge. What it carries is billed as data transfer.

choices.text: It has no zone of its own and no hourly price
choices.why: Right. One per VPC, run by AWS across the region, and the bill sees only the bytes.

choices.text: It filters connections from outside, like a firewall
choices.why: It translates and forwards. Filtering is the security group's and the network ACL's job, in lesson 18.

prompt: Why can the six private subnets not simply share the `public` table?
hint: What would the internet gateway translate their addresses into?

choices.text: They have no public address for the gateway to use
choices.why: Right. The internet gateway maps a machine's private address to its own public one; with none, the packet has no way to come back. And a database should not be one route from the internet.

choices.text: A route table serves one subnet at most
choices.why: The `public` table serves three subnets. A table can serve many; a subnet uses one.

choices.text: A table cannot hold subnets of different tiers
choices.why: Tiers are names in the shop's plan. A route table knows nothing about them.

choices.text: The internet gateway accepts traffic from one zone only
choices.why: It serves the whole VPC across every zone; that is why one table serves `public-a`, `public-b` and `public-c`.

prompt: Why is `nat-a` created in `public-a` rather than in `app-a`, beside the machines it serves?
hint: The gateway's own packets are routed too.

choices.text: A NAT gateway in a private subnet would be reachable from the internet
choices.why: It is the other way round: in a private subnet it could not reach the internet at all.

choices.text: Its own packets are routed by its subnet's table, and only the public one has a way out
choices.why: Right. That is the second hop of the third packet: `public-a`'s table sends it to the internet gateway.

choices.text: Public subnets are cheaper per hour
choices.why: A subnet has no price. The NAT gateway costs the same 0.093 an hour wherever it sits.

choices.text: AWS keeps the private subnets free for machines
choices.why: There is no such rule; the reason is routing, not reservation.

prompt: A NAT gateway lets the shop's application call out and lets nobody call in. Why does nothing from outside get in?
hint: Think about what the gateway knows when a packet arrives that nobody asked for.

choices.text: It inspects each packet and drops the dangerous ones
choices.why: It inspects nothing. It is a translator, and the filters are lesson 18.

choices.text: Its Elastic IP refuses inbound traffic
choices.why: An address refuses nothing; it is a label. The reason is what the gateway can map the packet to.

choices.text: It has no way to know which private machine an unsolicited packet is for
choices.why: Right. A reply matches a connection somebody inside opened; a new connection from outside matches nothing, so it goes nowhere.

choices.text: Its route table has no route back to the internet
choices.why: It does: `public-a`'s table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to the internet gateway, which is how the shop's calls get out.

prompt: A machine in `app-a` calls the payment provider at `198.51.100.7`. Put the steps of the packet's way out in order.
hint: Two tables are read, one after the other.
items: `nat-a` puts its own public address in place of the machine's
`public-a`'s table matches `0.0.0.0/0` and sends it to the internet gateway
the internet gateway hands it to the internet
trap: The address is swapped by the NAT gateway, so it happens between the two tables.

prompt: A route table holds `0.0.0.0/0` to `nat-a`, `192.168.0.0/16` to the virtual private gateway, and `192.168.4.0/24` to a peering connection, `pcx-…`. Where does a packet for `192.168.4.20` go?
hint: Three routes contain the address. Compare their prefixes.

choices.text: To the virtual private gateway, the office's route
choices.why: The `/16` contains the address, and so does a longer route. The longer one wins.

choices.text: To the peering connection
choices.why: Right. `192.168.4.0/24` is the most specific route that contains `192.168.4.20`; the order the routes were written in does not matter.

choices.text: To `nat-a`, since `0.0.0.0/0` matches every address
choices.why: It matches, and it is the shortest prefix there is, so it loses to any other route that matches.

choices.text: Nowhere: two routes overlap, so the table is refused
choices.why: Overlapping routes are allowed and normal; only two routes for the same destination are refused.

prompt: In the same table, a packet goes to `192.168.9.1`. What is the prefix length of the route that carries it?
A private subnet's machines have IPv6 addresses and must reach the internet over IPv6 without being reachable from it. What does `::/0` point at?
hint: IPv6 needs no translation.

choices.text: The zone's NAT gateway, as for IPv4
choices.why: A NAT gateway translates private IPv4 addresses. An IPv6 address is already public and needs only a one-way door.

choices.text: The internet gateway
choices.why: That would make the subnet public over IPv6: connections could be opened to its machines from outside.

choices.text: An egress-only internet gateway
choices.why: Right. It lets connections out over IPv6 and none in, and it has no hourly charge.

choices.text: The virtual private gateway, which keeps traffic private
choices.why: A virtual private gateway is the VPC's end of a VPN to the office (lesson 24), not a way to the internet.

prompt: moto stored every route of the lesson. What does that prove about where a packet goes?
hint: What does moto carry?

choices.text: That the path works, since moto would refuse a broken route
choices.why: moto refuses some malformed requests, such as a duplicate destination, but it never sends a packet down a route.

choices.text: Nothing: moto routes no packet
choices.why: Right. On AWS, Reachability Analyzer checks a path from the configuration and Flow Logs record what moved; neither was run here.

choices.text: That AWS would route the same way, because moto is AWS's code
choices.why: moto is an independent open-source imitation of AWS's API, not AWS's code.

choices.text: That the NAT gateway is up, since its state is `available`
choices.why: The state is a field in a record. In moto there is no gateway behind it to be up or down.

prompt: With the prices of the lesson and 730 hours in a month, how many dollars a month do TWO NAT gateways cost, each with its Elastic IP, before any traffic?
hint: 0.093 and 0.005 an hour, for each of two.

prompt: The shop moves from three NAT gateways to one shared one, with the same 200 GB a month going out. Which line of the bill does NOT change?
hint: One of the three prices is per gigabyte, whatever the number of gateways.

choices.text: The hours of NAT gateway
choices.why: Those fall from three gateways' worth to one: 203.67 a month to 67.89.

choices.text: The hours of public IPv4 address, since each gateway kept its own
choices.why: Two Elastic IPs go with the two gateways, so that line falls too.

choices.text: The gigabytes processed by NAT
choices.why: Right. 200 × 0.093 = 18.60 whether one gateway carries them or three share them.

choices.text: The data transfer between zones
choices.why: That one appears: zones b and c now cross into zone a for every gigabyte.

prompt: A different shop runs one shared NAT gateway, and 10 TB a month (10,240 GB) of its NAT traffic comes from the two zones without the gateway. On money alone, which arrangement is cheaper?
hint: Compare the crossing at 0.02 a gigabyte with the 143.08 that two more gateways cost.

choices.text: The shared gateway, since a gateway costs more than any crossing
choices.why: At this volume the crossing is 10,240 × 0.02 = 204.80 a month, more than the 143.08 the extra gateways cost.

choices.text: One per zone: the crossing would cost 204.80 a month, more than 143.08
choices.why: Right. The break-even was about 7,154 GB a month; 10,240 is past it, so three gateways win on money as well as on failure.

choices.text: They cost the same, since processing is per gigabyte either way
choices.why: Processing is the same either way, but the hours and the crossing are not, and they are what the comparison is about.

choices.text: The shared gateway, because the crossing is free inside a region
choices.why: Between two zones of a region is 0.01 a gigabyte each way, as lesson 1 measured. Only within one zone is it free.

prompt: Sharing one NAT gateway saves the shop about 140 dollars a month. Why does production still use three?
hint: What happens to zones b and c when zone a fails?

choices.text: A failure of zone a would also cut b and c off from the internet
choices.why: Right. The shop spread across zones to survive losing one; a shared gateway undoes that for every outbound call.

choices.text: A NAT gateway carries traffic from its own zone only
choices.why: It carries traffic from any subnet whose table points at it; the shared design depends on exactly that.

choices.text: The crossing between zones would cost more than the gateways at 200 GB
choices.why: At 200 GB the crossing is about 2.67 dollars a month. Money favours sharing; the reason is the failure.

choices.text: AWS requires one NAT gateway per zone in production accounts
choices.why: AWS requires nothing of the kind; staging shares one in the same organisation. It is the shop's decision.

prompt: Match each line of the price list to its price in São Paulo, from the offers the lesson read.
hint: Two of them are the same number in different units.

prompt: After both scripts, somebody creates a subnet `cache-a` in zone a and associates nothing with it. Where can its machines send packets?
hint: Which table does an unassociated subnet use, and what is in it now?

choices.text: To the internet through `nat-a`, like the other subnets of zone a
choices.why: Being in zone a gives it nothing; `private-a` serves the subnets associated with it, and `cache-a` is not one.

choices.text: To the internet through the internet gateway, since a new subnet starts public
choices.why: A new subnet starts in the main table, and the shop's main table has no way out.

choices.text: Inside the VPC and nowhere else
choices.why: Right. It uses the main table, which holds only `local`. That is the safe default the lesson set up on purpose.

choices.text: Nowhere, until a table is associated
choices.why: The main table still gives it `local`, so it reaches every other subnet of the VPC.

prompt: Which of these hold for the shop's VPC after `16-vpc.sh` and `17-routes.sh`? Choose all that apply.
hint: The last transcript lists every table.

choices.text: One table, `public`, serves the three public subnets
choices.why: Right. Three associations, and `0.0.0.0/0` to the internet gateway.

choices.text: `app-b` reaches the internet through `nat-a`
choices.why: `app-b` uses `private-b`, which points at `nat-b`. Nothing crosses a zone.

choices.text: The main table serves no subnet
choices.why: Right. Its single association is the marker that makes it main.

choices.text: Each private table serves two subnets
choices.why: Right. The zone's `app` and `data` subnets.

choices.text: The private tables route `192.168.0.0/16` to the office
choices.why: That route was added by hand to be read, and the script leaves it out.

prompt: A machine in `app-c` calls a payment provider. Its packet is routed first by `private-c`, which hands it to the NAT gateway called ___.
hint: Each zone has its own, named after the zone's letter.
